text:
Dear Dr. Morrison,

Thank you for evaluating Arthur, a 2-year, 6-month-old boy referred for a comprehensive orthopedic assessment. Arthur was born at 39 weeks gestation via uncomplicated spontaneous vaginal delivery from a cephalic lie, with no breech presentation noted during pregnancy or delivery. 

At birth, a cleft of the secondary palate was immediately identified, alongside rigid equinovarus foot contractures. Subsequent neonatal examinations confirmed congenital dislocations involving both hips as well as true dislocations of the knee joints bilaterally. Orthopedic skeletal surveys revealed hypoplastic, underdeveloped cervical vertebral bodies; reassuringly, serial cervical films confirm an absence of cervical kyphosis, and the remainder of the spine demonstrates no scoliosis. Radiographs of his hands and feet additionally revealed supernumerary ossification centers within the carpus along with noticeably shortened metatarsals bilaterally.

Arthur is otherwise in good spirits and is achieving his expected cognitive and communicative milestones. A screening echocardiogram completed last year was entirely normal, and he has passed both vision and hearing assessments. He lives at home with his parents and older sister, and the family history is unremarkable for any connective tissue or bone health conditions. He takes no prescription medications other than daily over-the-counter vitamin D drops.

Given these complex congenital joint and vertebral findings, I would value your expert input regarding his structural management.

Sincerely,
Dr. Clara Evans
General Pediatrics
